docs.title: trust-ledger-ui
docs.text: A local web page for the trust ledger of a paper project. Browse every claim of your papers, see which have no attestation or a stale one, read what would be signed, and attest one claim or many at once, with the same reason, signed through your ssh-agent.

docs.title: What it does
docs.text:
You want to … Page see which results of which paper still need an attestation A tour of the page attest one claim, or a whole selection, with one reason Attest claims attest that a hypothesis is a known theorem Attest a hypothesis find out what changed since you signed Snapshots and diffs read the paper statement next to the formal statement A tour of the page, Review packs run lock, verify, check, extract without a terminal Background jobs

The page renders the mathematics (KaTeX), so reading before signing happens where you sign. Nothing is signed that you have not seen in the preview, and every signature is made by your own key through your own ssh-agent.

docs.title: What you need
docs.text: Short version: Python 3.11 with uv, a checkout of trust-ledger, a project that has a ledger/ledger.toml, and, for attesting, an SSH key that is registered in the ledger and loaded in your agent. The details, per task, are on Before you start.

docs.title: Where to begin
docs.text:
1. Before you start: what each task needs.
  2. Install and first start: five minutes.
  3. Setting up signing: once per person.
  4. Attest claims: the everyday workflow.

Written for

Authors of papers that use a trust ledger: you write the paper (and perhaps its Lean formalisation) and you are one of the people who vouch for its results. You do not need to know how the ledger works inside; the documentation of the trust-ledger repository explains the method.

Status

Version 0.0.1, written alongside trust-ledger 0.3.0 (ledger format 0.3.0). It needs a ledger.py that has the library API this tool uses (status --json, claim_detail, diff_since and so on); the manual says where that matters.

docs.title: After you edited the paper
docs.text:
Prerequisites

A project whose ledger the tool can read (install). For re-attesting also a loaded key (signing); for the Lean step, whatever your project's extract needs; for packs, LaTeX.

Whenever the paper's statements, the Lean code or the evidence behind a claim change, the claims that rest on it become stale. This page is the routine for that situation. Pick the steps that apply.

edit → (Lean changed?  run extract) → Reload → read what changed → [review pack] → attest again → lock → rebuild the paper

docs.title: 1. Let the ledger see the change
docs.text:
• You edited the LaTeX of a paper: nothing to do. The page notices on its own.
  • You changed the Lean code: the ledger reads Lean through an extracted dump. Run Run… → extract Lean evidence (jobs). It runs your project's extractor (for Lean, Docker; it takes minutes, so it asks first).

docs.title: 2. Reload
docs.text:
The amber bar appears within about five seconds of a change on disk:

Press Reload now. The ledger is read again (a few seconds). The counts change: claims that depend on what you edited are now stale.

docs.title: 3. Read what changed
docs.text:
Select a stale claim. Under What changed since the attestation you see the difference between what was attested and what is there now:

Removed text is red, new text green. Under it, changed evidence (for example the type or value of a Lean declaration it depends on). The first sentence says which attestation it is compared with. How this works, and why it is sometimes unavailable, is on Snapshots and diffs.

docs.title: 4. Decide
docs.text:
• The change is harmless (a typo, a comment): attest again, with a reason such as "wording only".
  • The change matters: read the claim again, and the claims that use it. Build a review pack for the stale claims to read them side by side with their formal statements.

docs.title: 5. Attest again
docs.text: Select the claims, mark them seen, attest: Attest claims. A new attestation is bound to the new state. Older attestations stay in the history and are shown as stale.

docs.title: After attesting
docs.text:
Attestations and evidence enter the root hash that the paper prints. To make the paper agree with the ledger:

  1. Run… → write the lock file (lock), then verify to check it (jobs).
  2. On the command line, regenerate the files the paper includes, then rebuild the paper:
python3 path/to/ledger.py -P NAME tex

(ledger.py status prints a note when the root in the paper's generated file is older than the ledger's.)

Why the second step is not a button

The tex command writes into your paper's source tree. The tool leaves that to you for now.

docs.title: Attest claims
docs.text:
Prerequisites

  • The tool runs and shows your paper (install).
  • Your key is registered in the ledger and loaded in your ssh-agent (signing).
  • You have read the claims you are about to attest. The tool helps you remember which ones you read; it cannot read for you.

An attestation says: this person has examined this statement, in this state, at this level of confidence, for this reason. Each one is bound to the exact state of the statement and of the evidence behind it. If either changes, the attestation becomes stale and the claim shows up again under needs attention.

docs.title: Levels
docs.text:
The ledger knows three levels, green, yellow and conjecture. What each means for your paper is for your project to agree on (the ledger itself only demands that a yellow attestation has a reason). A common reading:

Level Typical use Reason green you have checked it and vouch for it optional yellow you vouch for it with a reservation or after a lighter check required conjecture you record it as a conjecture, not as established optional

Your project may define a checklist (items such as "re-ran the machine check myself"). Ticked items are part of what is signed.

docs.title: One claim
docs.text:
1. Click the claim in the list. Read the statement, the back-translation and the Lean statement, if there are any.
  2. Press Mark as seen (v). The claim gets a ✓ in the list.
  3. Press Attest… (a).
  4. Choose level, enter a reason, tick checklist items, check the key.
  5. Review, then Sign.

docs.title: Many claims with one reason
docs.text:
1. Narrow the list: the filter (needs attention, no attestation, stale …) and the search box.
  2. Use Select…: all shown, all stale, all without attestation, shown, not yet seen, or clear selection. You can also tick rows, press x, or use the checkbox in the table header for everything shown.
  3. Read them. Next unseen opens the next selected claim you have not marked; press v when you have read it. The bar shows N selected, M seen.
  4. Press Attest N selected….

The loop that works

Filter to stale, Select… → all stale, build a review pack for the selection, read it, mark the claims seen, attest.

docs.title: The dialog
docs.text:
• Level and Reason. Templates under the reason field fill it in: the ones from your config and your most recent reasons. One reason applies to the whole batch.
  • Checklist. The items that apply to claims.
  • Key. The registered keys, with a note if one is not in your agent (see).

docs.title: Review: what will be signed
docs.text:
Pressing Review asks the server to check everything and show a summary. Nothing is signed yet.

  • the person, the key and its fingerprint, and how many signatures (and agent prompts) to expect;
  • the exact reason text that will be signed;
  • a table of the claims: what each has now, the bound hash (the state being attested), and whether you marked it as seen;
  • problems per claim (a wrong checklist item, for example). Claims with a problem are left out.

Claims you did not mark as seen are listed in an amber box. You can still sign them, but only after ticking I am attesting claims I have not marked as seen. It is a warning, not a block; the decision is yours. If you change anything in the dialog, the review is discarded and you review again.

docs.title: Sign
docs.text:
Sign N attestation(s) starts the job. For each claim in turn, the server

  1. checks that the statement and its evidence are still exactly what the review showed, and skips the claim if not;
  2. asks your ssh-agent for a signature (confirm there if your agent asks) and verifies it;
  3. appends the record to ledger/attestations.toml and records a snapshot.

A failure on one claim does not stop the others; the result table says what happened to each (attested, skipped, failed). Attested claims leave the selection.

docs.title: Undo
docs.text: Right after a batch, Undo this batch removes exactly the records it appended from attestations.toml, provided nothing else has changed that file since. After that, or after you close the dialog and do something else to the file, remove records by hand.

docs.title: What stays in your hands
docs.text:
• Seen is your mark: it is kept in this browser, per claim and state, and is not written to the ledger. It does not prove you read anything; it helps you remember.
  • Each signature is made by your key, through your agent, on your say-so.
  • Every action is logged to ledger-ui.log next to the config file.

Next: after you sign, update the lock file (jobs) and rebuild the paper, as in After you edited the paper.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
The tool reads one file, ledger-ui.toml. It holds where the ledger is and who you are, nothing about the project: the papers, the checklist and the review settings come from the project's own ledger/ledger.toml. Create it with ledger-ui --init (install).

Where it is looked for: --config FILE; else ./ledger-ui.toml; else ~/.config/trust-ledger-ui/config.toml ($XDG_CONFIG_HOME is respected). Paths in it are relative to the config file.

Unknown tables or keys are an error, so a typo cannot pass silently.

docs.title: Reference
docs.text:
[ledger]
file = "../project/ledger/ledger.toml"   # required
tool = "../trust-ledger/ledger.py"       # required

[signing]
person = "Your Name"                     # shown in the header; the signing person comes from keys.toml
key = "yourid"                           # default key: its id in ledger/keys.toml
reasons = ["Checked against the paper and the Lean statement"]   # templates offered in the attest dialog

[metadata]
paper_toml = "paper/{name}/paper.toml"   # optional: titles and PDF links

[viewer]
pdf = "embed"                            # accepted; has no effect yet (packs are always shown in the page)

[server]
port = 0                                 # 0: a free port; set a number to have the same address every time
open_browser = true
Key Default Meaning [ledger] file required the project's ledger/ledger.toml; the project root is two levels up [ledger] tool required a trust-ledger ledger.py with the library API; see requirements [signing] key first key of the ledger key id preselected in the dialog [signing] reasons none templates under the reason field [metadata] paper_toml none pattern for a paper's paper.toml, relative to the project root; {name} is the paper's name in the ledger [server] port 0 0 picks a free port; see From another device for a fixed one [server] open_browser true open the browser at start

docs.title: paper.toml
docs.text: If paper_toml is set and the file exists, the page shows the paper's title in the paper menu and links to its PDFs: the paper itself and, if the file's [editions] table names them, the reviewed and explained editions. Only files that exist are linked. The file is the one your publishing workflow already uses; the tool reads [paper] title, main and [editions] and ignores the rest. It warns if name or main disagrees with the ledger.

docs.title: Command line
docs.text: Option Effect --config FILE use this config file --init LEDGER_TOML write ./ledger-ui.toml for that ledger and exit; never overwrites --summary print the papers with their counts and exit (no server) --no-browser print the address without opening the browser

docs.title: Files
docs.text: Next to the config file: ledger-ui.log (one JSON line per signing, skip, failure or undo) and .ledger-ui/packs/ (review packs). In the project: ledger/attestations.toml, ledger/snapshots/, and what the jobs write (Security and what is written).

docs.title: Attest a hypothesis
docs.text:
Prerequisites

As for attesting claims: a registered key, loaded in your ssh-agent.

Some results are proved given a hypothesis, typically a known theorem from the literature that is not formalised in the project. The ledger lists it as a hypothesis and records who has checked that it really is that known theorem.

docs.title: Steps
docs.text:
1. Open the Hypotheses tab (or press t). The list shows each hypothesis with its status: known theorem, stale or not attested.
  2. Click one. You see its statement (from the paper if the paper states it, otherwise the hand-written text), the cited sources as links, what attesting it means, its attestations, and the results that are proved given it.
  3. Open the cited source and check it. The checklist of your project says what to check, typically: found the cited statement in the source; compared it with the formal definition and with the paper's statement; checked that the conditions match (objects, field, symmetry, order).
  4. Mark as seen, then Attest as a known theorem…. The dialog is the one from attesting claims, with the checklist for hypotheses. A green attestation means: this is a known theorem.
  5. Review, sign.

The list of results that are proved given it links to those claims.

The same hypothesis can look different in different papers

A hypothesis has one statement per scope. If one paper states the lemma and another only cites it, the second one uses the hand-written text of the ledger entry, which has a different hash. An attestation made in the first paper then shows as stale when you look at the second. That is the ledger's rule: you attest the statement as it is used where you look.

docs.title: Install and first start
docs.text:
Prerequisites

Python 3.11+, uv, a trust-ledger checkout, a project with ledger/ledger.toml (details).

docs.title: 1. Get the two repositories
docs.text:
Put them next to each other (the tests expect that; the tool itself only needs the path to ledger.py).

git clone https://github.com/HansAschauer/trust-ledger.git
git clone git@github.com:HansAschauer/trust-ledger-ui.git
cd trust-ledger-ui
uv sync

uv sync creates a virtual environment. The tool itself has no runtime dependencies (Python's standard library only); the JavaScript it needs is included in the repository.

docs.title: 2. Write the configuration once
docs.text:
Go to the directory where you want the config file to live (the project root is a good place) and run:

uv run ledger-ui --init path/to/your/project/ledger/ledger.toml

This writes ledger-ui.toml into the current directory:

[ledger]
file = "../your-project/ledger/ledger.toml"
tool = "../trust-ledger/ledger.py"   # a trust-ledger ledger.py with the library API

[signing]
person = "Your Name"
key = "yourkey"   # id in ledger/keys.toml; signs through ssh-agent

[metadata]
# paper_toml = "paper/{name}/paper.toml"   # titles and edition PDFs, if you have such files

It finds ledger.py in ledger/vendor/ of the project or in a trust-ledger directory next to it, and takes the first key of ledger/keys.toml as the signing key. Change anything that is not right. Paths are relative to the config file. The command never overwrites an existing file. All keys are described in Configuration.

docs.title: 3. Check that the tool can read the ledger
docs.text:
$ uv run ledger-ui --summary
nuclear      claims  32  none  13  stale   9  green   1  yellow   9  hypotheses open 0/1
threshold    claims  23  none   9  stale  10  green   0  yellow   4  hypotheses open 1/1

One line per paper. The first call takes a few seconds per paper, because the ledger parses the papers.

docs.title: 4. Start
docs.text:
uv run ledger-ui

It prints an address and opens your browser:

ledger-ui: http://127.0.0.1:41873/#Xq3…

The part after # is an access token

The server listens on 127.0.0.1 only, and every request needs the token. The page keeps it for the session and removes it from the address bar. If you close the tab, use the printed address again. --no-browser prints it without opening a browser; Ctrl+C stops the server.

Where the config file is searched: --config FILE, then ./ledger-ui.toml, then ~/.config/trust-ledger-ui/config.toml.

docs.title: 5. The first screen
docs.text:
On the first start the page may offer to record snapshots (the blue bar in the picture on the home page). That is explained in Snapshots and diffs; you can do it right away.

Next: Setting up signing, unless you only want to browse.

docs.title: Background jobs
docs.text:
Prerequisites

Nothing beyond a working tool, except what the job itself needs: LaTeX for review packs, the project's extractor (for Lean: Docker) for extract.

Some ledger.py commands take a while. The tool runs them in the background, shows their output as it appears, and keeps working while they run.

docs.title: Start one
docs.text:
The Run… menu in the header offers:

Entry Runs Effect verify the lock file ledger.py [-P paper] verify recomputes the root and compares it with the lock file write the lock file ledger.py [-P paper] lock writes lock.json (or lock-NAME.json for a selected paper) run the checks ledger.py check runs the project's [check.*] commands and records the results extract Lean evidence (Docker) ledger.py extract runs the extractors of all adapters and writes their dumps; asks first, takes minutes

Review pack is started from the claim list (Review packs).

With a paper selected, lock and verify apply to that paper; with all papers they apply to the whole ledger.

docs.title: Watch and control
docs.text: Jobs in the header opens the panel at the bottom. Each row shows what ran, its state (running, done, failed, cancelled), how long it took, and links: log (the output, streamed while it runs), open pack (for review packs) and cancel (for a running job).

docs.title: Rules
docs.text:
• One job per kind at a time. Starting a second verify while one runs is refused with a message.
  • Only one Lean job at all. extract starts Docker Lean, which does not run twice in parallel.
  • extract is never started automatically, and always asks.
  • The tool starts only these commands, with arguments it builds from checked names. The page cannot send a command line.
  • After lock, check or extract finish, the page reloads the ledger, because they changed files it reads.

A job that fails shows its exit status and its output; the output usually says why.

docs.title: From another device
docs.text:
Prerequisites

SSH access from the other device to the machine where the tool runs, and a way to forward a port (the -L option of ssh, or the port-forwarding feature of your SSH app).

The tool never listens on a network interface: it binds to 127.0.0.1, and it rejects requests whose Host is anything but 127.0.0.1 or localhost with its own port. That is deliberate, because it can sign in your name. To use it from a laptop or a phone, bring the port to the device through an SSH tunnel.

docs.title: Steps
docs.text:
1. On the machine with the project, give the server a fixed port in ledger-ui.toml:
[server]
port = 8765
open_browser = false
  1. Start it there: uv run ledger-ui. Note the address with the token.
  2. On your device, open a tunnel with the same port on both sides:
ssh -L 8765:127.0.0.1:8765 you@the-machine
  1. In the browser of your device, open http://127.0.0.1:8765/#TOKEN (the token from step 2).

Signing happens where the tool runs

The ssh-agent that signs is the one in the environment the tool was started in, on that machine. Do not forward your agent to a machine you do not trust.

docs.title: On a phone
docs.text:
The page adapts to narrow screens: one column, a list with the claim and its attestation, the detail below it, and a dialog that fits the screen.

Reading, selecting, marking as seen and attesting all work with touch. Keyboard shortcuts need a keyboard.

docs.title: Before you start
docs.text: What you need depends on what you want to do. Find your task in the table; each page of the manual repeats its own prerequisites at the top.

docs.title: Requirements per task
docs.text:
Task You need Run the tool at all Python 3.11 or newer, uv, a checkout of trust-ledger (its ledger.py), a project with ledger/ledger.toml, a modern browser Browse claims and hypotheses, read statements, filter, search nothing more Attest (one or many) an SSH key that is registered in the ledger (ledger.py addkey), loaded in your ssh-agent, and listed in the project's ledger/keys.toml with your name Review packs (PDF) latexmk and pdflatex, and a paper that builds; back-translations appear in the pack if the ledger has a [review] section Jobs lock, verify, check nothing more (check runs whatever the project's [check.*] entries say) Job extract whatever the project's adapter needs (for Lean: Docker and the project's dump.sh) Paper titles and PDF links a paper.toml per paper (optional) Diffs of what changed snapshots, which are written whenever the tool attests; for older attestations record them once, see here

The vendored ledger.py of an older project

Many projects keep a copy of ledger.py under ledger/vendor/. A copy made before 2026-11-06 lacks the library API this tool uses. Either copy the current ledger.py from trust-ledger into the project, or point the tool at a trust-ledger checkout with [ledger] tool = "…/trust-ledger/ledger.py" (what ledger-ui --init does when it finds one). The error message says "lacks the library API" when this is the problem.

No ledger yet?

Run python3 path/to/trust-ledger/ledger.py init in the project directory. It finds your paper, writes ledger/ with a claim for every labelled theorem, lemma and so on, and can register your SSH key (--key ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub --person "Your Name"). Then continue with Install and first start. ledger-ui --init is a different command: it writes the tool's own configuration file for a ledger that already exists.

docs.title: A checklist before the first attestation
docs.text:
• [ ] uv run ledger-ui --summary lists your papers with their counts (the tool can read the ledger).
  • [ ] ssh-add -l shows your key (the agent holds it).
  • [ ] The key's id appears in ledger/keys.toml with person = "Your Name".
  • [ ] You can open a claim and read its statement (rendering works).

If one of these fails, Troubleshooting has the message and the fix.

docs.title: Which page next?
docs.text:
I am newI edited the paper or the Lean codeI want to attest what I have readI want to see what changed since I signed

Install and first start, then Setting up signing.

After you edited the paper.

Attest claims.

Snapshots and diffs.

docs.title: Review packs
docs.text:
Prerequisites

latexmk and pdflatex, and a paper that builds. One paper must be selected in the paper menu (a pack belongs to one paper). Back-translations of the formal statements appear in the pack if the ledger's [review] section names them.

A review pack is a PDF that puts what you are about to vouch for side by side: the claims' statements from the paper, the back-translations of the formal (Lean) statements, and the Lean text, with the definitions they use gathered once. It also covers what the claims rest on (the claims they use and the Lean steps). It is made by the ledger's own review command; the tool runs it for you and shows the result.

docs.title: Build one
docs.text:
• For one claim: open it and press Review pack.
  • For several: select them (Attest claims) and press Review pack in the bar above the table.

The pack is built as a background job: the paper is built once for its numbers and references, then the pack twice. A small paper needs ten seconds; a large one minutes. The job's log is in the Jobs panel, and the PDF opens under the list when it is done. Open in a new tab gives you the browser's own viewer at full size; Close hides it.

docs.title: When a pack is out of date
docs.text: If a claim in the pack changes after the pack was built, the viewer shows an amber note older than the statement of …. Build it again. It compares the claims you selected; a change to something they only rest on is not detected, so rebuild after larger edits.

docs.title: Where the files go
docs.text: .ledger-ui/packs/<job id>/ next to your config file (the PDF and the LaTeX of the body). The project's own review/ directory is not touched, so a pack made here never overwrites one you made by hand. Add .ledger-ui/ to your ignore file.

docs.title: Typical loop
docs.text:
1. Filter to stale, select them all.
  2. Review pack, read it.
  3. Mark the claims seen, Attest N selected….

docs.title: Security and what is written
docs.text: The tool can sign attestations in your name, so its defaults are strict. This page says what it does, and what it writes.

docs.title: What protects it
docs.text:
• Local only. The server listens on 127.0.0.1. Requests with another Host header are refused (this stops DNS-rebinding tricks from other websites), and so are requests with a foreign Origin.
  • A token per start. Every call to the API needs the random token printed at start. It travels in the address after #, which a browser never sends to a server, and the page forwards it in a header and removes it from the address bar.
  • Nothing is signed that you did not review. Signing takes only the id of a review you have seen. The server computes the state being attested itself, and skips a claim whose state changed after your review.
  • Signing only through ssh-agent. The tool never asks for a passphrase and never opens a private key file. It copies the public key to a scratch directory for the signing call, so ssh-keygen cannot fall back to the private key next to it.
  • No outside scripts. The JavaScript (Alpine.js, KaTeX) is part of the repository, with versions and checksums in src/trust_ledger_ui/static/VENDOR.md. The page loads nothing from the network, and a strict content-security policy allows only its own files (unsafe-eval is needed because Alpine compiles its expressions; only same-origin scripts may run).
  • A fixed list of jobs. The page cannot send a command line or a path; the server builds the arguments from checked names.

docs.title: What it does not protect against
docs.text: Anyone who can already run programs as you can use your ssh-agent anyway, and can read the token from the process list. On a shared machine, other users can connect to the port but need the token. Keep the agent's keys protected by a passphrase, and use ssh-add -c if you want a confirmation for every signature.

docs.title: What is written, and where
docs.text:
File Written by Contents ledger/attestations.toml Sign (appends); Undo (removes the last batch) the attestation records ledger/snapshots/<hash>.json signing; Record snapshots now what an attestation bound to (Snapshots) ledger/lock*.json, ledger/checks.json, ledger/lean.json jobs lock, check, extract the files ledger.py itself writes for those commands ledger-ui.log (next to the config) every signing, skip, failure and undo one JSON line each: time, claim, level, key, person, state hash .ledger-ui/packs/ (next to the config) review packs the PDFs and their LaTeX body (in the browser) Mark as seen which claims you marked, per claim and state; not shared, not in the ledger

Everything else about the ledger stays as it is on disk. The tool keeps no database and makes no network connections other than its own page.

docs.title: Setting up signing
docs.text:
Prerequisites

OpenSSH (ssh-keygen, ssh-agent, ssh-add) and a project whose ledger you may add a key to. Needed once per person, only if you want to attest; browsing needs none of it.

An attestation is a statement by a named person, signed with that person's SSH key. The tool signs through your ssh-agent. It never asks for a passphrase and never reads a private key file; the agent holds the unlocked key and makes the signature. That is why the setup below matters.

docs.title: 1. A key with a passphrase
docs.text:
If you have no key for this purpose yet:

ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -C "you@example.org" -f ~/.ssh/id_ed25519_ledger

Choose a passphrase. A key without one lets anyone who can read the file sign as you.

docs.title: 2. Register the key in the ledger
docs.text:
Once per person and project, from the project root:

python3 path/to/trust-ledger/ledger.py addkey yourid --person "Your Name" --pub ~/.ssh/id_ed25519_ledger.pub

yourid is a short name for the key; it appears in the tool's key menu and in ledger/keys.toml. The person's name is what appears under every attestation. Commit ledger/keys.toml with the project; it holds public keys only.

docs.title: 3. Load the key into the agent
docs.text:
At the start of each session:

ssh-add ~/.ssh/id_ed25519_ledger
ssh-add -l          # the key is listed

To have the agent load keys on first use, put this in ~/.ssh/config:

Host *
    AddKeysToAgent yes

No agent running?

Most desktop environments start one. In a plain terminal: eval "$(ssh-agent -s)", then ssh-add. The tool reads SSH_AUTH_SOCK from the environment it was started in, so start ledger-ui from the same session.

docs.title: 4. Tell the tool which key to use
docs.text:
In ledger-ui.toml:

[signing]
key = "yourid"

The dialog lets you choose another registered key; the config only sets the default. The person is taken from ledger/keys.toml, not from the config.

docs.title: What you will see
docs.text:
When you open the attest dialog, each key shows whether the agent holds it:

If the selected key is not in agent, the dialog tells you to run ssh-add; nothing can be signed until the agent has it. Press Review again afterwards.

docs.title: One signature per attestation
docs.text: Every attestation is signed by its own ssh-keygen call. If you use an agent that asks for confirmation on every use (ssh-add -c), expect one prompt per claim, and the review step tells you how many. That is intended: a signature should be deliberate, and the tool never bundles or caches one.

docs.title: Snapshots and diffs
docs.text:
Prerequisites

None for reading a diff. To have diffs for attestations you made before this feature existed, record snapshots once (below).

When a claim becomes stale, the ledger can say that it changed, because an attestation stores only a hash of what it bound to. To say what changed, the tool needs the text from the time of the attestation. That is a snapshot.

docs.title: What a snapshot is
docs.text:
A small file ledger/snapshots/<bound-hash>.json, written whenever the tool (or ledger.py attest) records an attestation. It holds the statement text, the evidence behind the claim with its content (for a Lean declaration: its type and value, and the declarations it depends on), and the statements of the claims it uses.

  • It is not part of the ledger's hashes or its root; deleting it changes nothing about what is attested.
  • It is named by the hash, so one file serves all attestations of the same state.
  • Commit ledger/snapshots/ with the project, so that your co-authors can see the same diffs.

docs.title: The diff
docs.text:
For every claim or hypothesis with a stale attestation, the detail view shows What changed since the attestation, compared with the latest attestation that has a snapshot:

Part Shows statement a word-level difference of the LaTeX source (red removed, green added) uses claims it uses whose statement changed, with their difference evidence nodes each changed Lean declaration, file or citation, field by field. If only a dependency of a declaration changed, it says so

The line above the difference names the attestation it is compared with (person, date, level).

docs.title: Attestations without a snapshot
docs.text:
Attestations made before snapshots existed have none. The page shows a blue bar:

N current attestation(s) have no snapshot of what they bind to, so a later change cannot be shown as a diff. Record snapshots now

Pressing it writes a snapshot for every attestation that is current right now. On the command line: ledger.py snapshot. Do it while the attestations are current: that is the last moment the text they bound to is still available.

Stale already, no snapshot

If an attestation is stale and has no snapshot, the text it bound to is gone, and the page says so ("no snapshot was recorded … it cannot be compared"). You see that something changed, not what. Your version control, if the project uses one, may still hold the old text.

Standalone attestation files (ledger.py attest … --out) and attest --no-snapshot write no snapshot.

docs.title: Rebuilding snapshots from git
docs.text:
Prerequisites

The project is a git repository, and the attestation was committed. ledger.py with snapshot --from-git (trust-ledger from 2026-11-07).

For a stale attestation without a snapshot, the text it bound to may still be in your git history. A second blue bar then offers Rebuild from git (on the command line: ledger.py snapshot --from-git; add --dry-run to only look). For each attestation the tool finds the commit that added it, unpacks the project as it was, loads it and recomputes the claim's hash there. A snapshot is written only if that hash is exactly the attested one, so what you get is provably what was attested.

This works only if everything the ledger reads is in git. A generated file that is ignored, typically the Lean dump ledger/lean.json, is missing in the old state, the hash differs, and nothing is written. The bar then says how many could not be recovered. Two ways forward:

  • … also text only (--partial) keeps the statement text of the commit that added the attestation. It is marked as not verified in the page, and only the statement is compared, not the evidence. Useful for seeing how a wording changed.
  • For the future: commit the dumps, or rely on the snapshots that are now written at every attestation.

docs.title: Which commit was it?
docs.text: When a project is a git repository, every attestation also records the commit it was made at (git_head) and whether other tracked files differed from it (git_dirty). These two values are not signed and not hashed: they are a hint, because history can be rewritten. The diff shows them ("Attested at git commit …") together with the list of files that changed since, so you can continue with your usual git diff <commit>.

docs.title: A tour of the page
docs.text:
Prerequisites

The tool is running (install). Nothing else; this page is only about looking.

docs.title: The regions
docs.text:
Header. The project, the paper menu (with the paper's title if it has a paper.toml), counts for the paper, links to its PDFs, the person, the Run… menu for background jobs, Jobs, and Reload.

The counts:

Chip Meaning none claims without any attestation stale claims that have attestations, but none is current: the statement or what it rests on changed since current claims with at least one current attestation hypotheses open hypotheses nobody has attested as a known theorem (yet)

Claim list (left). Tabs Claims and Hypotheses. For claims: a filter (the default is needs attention: none plus stale), a search over names and labels, and columns for the attestation, the evidence class, where the statement comes from (tex or manual), the state of each tool (for example Lean) and the size of the register. Click a column header to sort. On a narrow screen only the claim and its attestation are shown.

Detail (right). The paper statement, the back-translation of the formal statement and the Lean statement if the project has them, the attestation history, what the claim uses and what uses it (click to jump), what it rests on, and, if it is stale, what changed.

docs.title: Assessments
docs.text:
If the ledger holds a model's assessment of a claim (a comparison of the paper text, the formal statement and its back-translation), the detail view shows its verdict and text, marked as by a model, an aid; not an attestation. A badge says whether it is still valid:

Badge Meaning current it records the claim's present statement (and back-translation) as what it judged outdated it judged an older state: the statement or something it rests on changed, or the back-translation was redone. Read the verdict as describing that older state unbound it was written before assessments recorded what they judged, so nothing can be said. ledger.py assess CLAIM --bind states that it still fits

For an unbound assessment in a project under git, the page compares with the history (a few seconds, once per paper): it shows From git: since it was written these changed: paper statement, back-translation …, or that none of the paper statement, the Lean references, the Lean extract and the back-translation changed (probably still describes the claim, which only you can confirm). The same list is ledger.py assess --audit; --bind-unchanged binds the unchanged ones.

The list filter assessment outdated or unbound collects the claims to look at. A new assessment is recorded with ledger.py assess CLAIM --verdict … --model … --notes-file …, which stores the state it judged.

docs.title: Reading what is shown
docs.text:
• Attestation column. The strongest current attestation, for instance green +1 (one more by someone else) or green · STALE (only stale ones).
  • ✓ after a name marks claims you have marked as seen in this browser.
  • Rendering. Formulas are drawn with KaTeX. A formula the renderer cannot draw is shown as source in red, with the reason as a tooltip, and the detail view lists how many there were. Unknown LaTeX commands in the text appear in amber. Nothing is hidden silently.

docs.title: Banners and messages
docs.text: Banner What it tells you Files changed on disk since this was loaded (amber) an input of the ledger changed; Reload now reads it again N current attestation(s) have no snapshot (blue) see Snapshots and diffs N ledger message(s) warnings and errors that ledger.py status prints, for example labelled results that are not in the ledger

docs.title: Keyboard
docs.text:
Shortcuts work when no text field has the focus. Every action also has a button.

Key Action j / k next / previous claim (or hypothesis) x add the current claim to the selection or remove it v mark the current claim as seen / not seen a attest the selection, or the current claim if nothing is selected t switch between claims and hypotheses

docs.title: Links you can bookmark
docs.text: ?paper=NAME&claim=NAME opens a paper and a claim directly. The address is kept up to date while you click, so reloading the page returns to where you were.

docs.title: What is not shown
docs.text: The tool shows the ledger as it is on disk. It keeps no database of its own; closing the tab loses nothing except the seen marks, which live in the browser.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text: Find the message, then the fix.

docs.title: Starting
docs.text: Message Cause and fix no ledger-ui.toml here and no ~/.config/…; use --config FILE no config found. Run ledger-ui --init …/ledger/ledger.toml in the directory you will start from, or pass --config unknown key(s) in [signing]: persn a typo in the config; the message lists the known keys … lacks the library API this UI needs the ledger.py named in [ledger] tool is too old. Point it at a current trust-ledger checkout, or copy the current ledger.py into the project (requirements) ledger format X; this UI supports 0.3.0 the ledger uses another format version than this version of the tool was tested with …/ledger.toml not found wrong [ledger] file; it must be the project's ledger/ledger.toml the page says No access token open the address that ledger-ui printed, including the part after # the page shows 401 or 403 the token is wrong (the server was restarted: use the new address), or you reached it under another host name. Use 127.0.0.1 or localhost

docs.title: Reading
docs.text: Symptom Cause and fix the first load takes seconds the ledger parses all papers; later requests are cached. The paper menu shows (loading…) meanwhile a formula appears in red as source the renderer does not know a macro or command. Hover for the reason. The paper's own \newcommands are taken from its preamble; exotic packages are not an amber word starting with \ in a statement an unknown LaTeX text command; it is shown as is Files changed on disk keeps coming back something rewrites a watched file (the ledger directory, the papers' .tex files, the review templates), for example a build that writes generated .tex files there

docs.title: Attesting
docs.text: Message Cause and fix not loaded in your ssh-agent: run ssh-add the key is not in the agent. ssh-add ~/.ssh/yourkey, then Review again (signing) no ssh-agent reachable (SSH_AUTH_SOCK) the tool was started where no agent runs. Start an agent, ssh-add, and start ledger-ui from that session the signature does not verify against the registered public key the key loaded in the agent is not the one registered under that id in ledger/keys.toml key … is not in ledger/keys.toml register it: ledger.py addkey ID --person "Name" --pub KEY.pub this preview is unknown or expired a review can be signed within 20 minutes, once. Press Review again another batch is still being signed wait for it to finish (it may be waiting for a confirmation in your agent) a claim is skipped: … changed since the preview its statement or evidence changed between your review and the signing. Review again yellow needs --reason write a reason, or choose another level checklist item(s) … not defined for this target the item does not apply to claims (or hypotheses); the message lists what is defined attestations.toml has changed since that batch Undo refuses when the file changed after your batch. Remove the records by hand

docs.title: Packs and jobs
docs.text:
Message Cause and fix needs one paper selected choose a paper in the paper menu (not all papers) the review pack did not build; see the job log open Jobs → log. Usually the paper does not build, or latexmk / pdflatex is missing a … job is already running / a Lean job is already running one job per kind, one Lean job overall; wait or cancel N not recoverable after Rebuild from git the old state is not fully in git (a generated, ignored file such as the Lean dump). Use also text only, or see Snapshots this project is not in a git repository the rebuild needs git; without it only snapshots made from now on exist no snapshot was recorded … cannot be compared the attestation is stale and was made before snapshots existed (Snapshots)

If something else goes wrong, ledger.py itself is the reference: run the same command in a terminal and compare (status, why CLAIM, diff CLAIM).

docs.title: Design decisions (2026-11-06)
docs.text: Settled in the planning discussion; the specification is in specification.

docs.title: Form
docs.text:
• Local web app (single page), not a TUI: attesting is mostly reading mathematics, and a terminal cannot render the formulas. A TUI can follow later on the same core.
  • Python standard library only (http.server, no framework), uv project, no npm and no build step. Vendored JavaScript in static/: Alpine.js (UI state), KaTeX (formulas). Flask/Starlette is the fallback if the hand-written routing becomes a burden; the core is kept independent of the server.
  • Core module (load ledger, compute status, write attestation, build review pack) without any UI.

docs.title: KaTeX, not MathJax
docs.text: Test over all 126 .tex files of the papers (9899 distinct formulas, 32 macros taken from the preambles): both engines render nearly everything. KaTeX is smaller (about 300 KB + 300 KB fonts vs 1.2 MB + 400 KB) and synchronous. Needed shims: \mathds -> \mathbb (both engines), \cite/\ref/\eqref as placeholders, psmallmatrix -> \bigl(\begin{smallmatrix}..\end{smallmatrix}\bigr), multline -> gather (KaTeX only). Do not enable MathJax's noundefined package (it hides unknown macros as red text). A formula that still does not render is shown as source with a note. Open: \mathbb{1} is a plain 1 in KaTeX; check by eye.

docs.title: Signing
docs.text: Only through ssh-agent (ssh-keygen -Y sign with the public key); the tool never asks for a passphrase and never reads a private key file. It warns when the configured key is not loaded. README must explain ssh-add / AddKeysToAgent yes for people who do not use an agent.

docs.title: Security of the local server
docs.text: 127.0.0.1 only; random token per start, required on every request that writes; check Host and Origin (DNS rebinding, CSRF); no third-party scripts (everything vendored).

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
• User/environment config (ledger-ui.toml: path to ledger.toml, person, key id, PDF viewer, reason templates). No project data is duplicated there.
  • Papers, [review] and [checklist.*] come from the ledger's ledger.toml.
  • Optional display metadata from paper/<name>/paper.toml (the publish workflow's file: title, [editions] -> links to the reviewed/explained PDFs), found through a configurable path pattern; missing file = fall back to the name. Not merged with the ledger configuration (separation of concerns); main is only cross-checked.

docs.title: Batch attestation
docs.text: Select claims, one dialog (level, reason, checklist, key), a preview table (old -> new, what is bound), then sign each. A claim counts as "seen" once it was opened in the detail view or marked explicitly; unseen claims in a batch are flagged: a warning plus an extra confirmation, no block (decided 2026-11-06). "Seen" is set only explicitly (click or key), never automatically. A failure on one claim does not abort the batch.

docs.title: Review packs
docs.text: First: a button that runs ledger.py review --for <selection> in the background and embeds the PDF next to the list. Later: inline view of statement / back-translation / Lean text. Wanted in ledger.py itself: "what changed since my attestation" (stale diff).

docs.title: trust-ledger-ui: specification (draft 1, 2026-11-06)
docs.text: Decisions behind this document: Design decisions. Everything here is open to correction before code.

docs.title: 1. Purpose and non-goals
docs.text:
Purpose: browse the trust ledger of a paper project (several papers), find claims and hypotheses that have no attestation or a stale one, read what would be signed, and attest one or many of them (same level, same reason) with an ssh-agent signature.

Non-goals: no editing of claims, citations or assertions (hand-edited TOML stays hand-edited); no verification logic of its own (that is ledger.py verify); no storage of ledger state outside the ledger's own files; no multi-user server (one person, one machine, 127.0.0.1).

docs.title: 2. Architecture
docs.text:
browser (Alpine.js + KaTeX, static/)  <--JSON/SSE-->  server.py (http.server, 127.0.0.1)
                                                          |
                                                      core/  (no HTTP, no UI)
                                                          |
                              ledger.py (imported as a module)   ssh-keygen / ssh-agent   latex (via ledger.py review)
  • core/ledgerio.py: the only module that touches ledger.py internals. Loads it from the configured path with importlib, checks __version__ and FORMAT_VERSION against a list of tested versions (warns on an untested one, refuses on a different format version). Exposes plain dataclasses: Paper, Claim, Hypothesis, Attestation. If ledger.py ever gets --json, only this module changes.
  • core/status.py: view model per claim (see 4). core/attest.py: validate, sign, append. core/jobs.py: background commands with a log. core/render.py: macro collection and shims for KaTeX.
  • The server is a thin layer; the whole core is testable without a browser.
  • Loading goes through Ledger(root, paper) once per paper and is cached with the mtime of every file the ledger read; a changed file invalidates the cache and the page shows "changed on disk, reload?".

docs.title: 3. Configuration: ledger-ui.toml
docs.text:
Looked up in this order: --config FILE, ./ledger-ui.toml, $XDG_CONFIG_HOME/trust-ledger-ui/config.toml. Paths are relative to the config file. The first start without a config offers to write one (asks for the ledger.toml path only).

[ledger]
file = "ledger/ledger.toml"                 # papers, [review], [checklist.*] come from here
tool = "ledger/vendor/ledger.py"            # imported as a module; also used for review/lock/verify/check/extract

[signing]
person = "Hans Aschauer"
key = "hans"                                # id in ledger/keys.toml; signs through ssh-agent only
reasons = ["Checked against blind backtranslation"]   # reason templates offered in the dialog

[metadata]                                  # optional, display and links only
paper_toml = "paper/{name}/paper.toml"      # title, [editions] -> links; missing file = name only

[viewer]
pdf = "xdg-open"                            # or "embed" (default) to show review packs in the page

[server]
port = 0                                    # 0 = free port; the URL with the token is printed
open_browser = true

No project data is copied into this file. Unknown keys are an error (typos must not be silent).

docs.title: 4. Data shown
docs.text: Per claim (from Ledger): name, paper(s), label, evidence class, statement source (tex/manual), per tool state (Lean ok/assumes (k/n known thm.), checks pass/fail), register size, attestations (latest per person: level, date, current/STALE, signature state), bound (current spec hash), uses / used-by. Derived attention: none (no attestation), stale (all attestations stale), ok. Per hypothesis: name, label, cites, known-theorem flag, attestations, checklist H1/H2. Per paper: counts (green, yellow, none, stale, failed checks, open hypotheses, uncovered labels), root hash, title and edition PDF links from paper.toml when present (cross-check: warn if its main differs). Ledger warnings and errors (as ledger.py status prints them) are shown in a collapsible bar.

docs.title: 5. Screens
docs.text:
One page, three regions: header (project, paper switcher, agent/key status, job indicator), list (left), detail (right). Keyboard shortcuts are optional extras; every action has a button.

  1. Papers: one row per paper with the counts; click selects the paper; "all papers" merges claims (shared claims appear once, with their papers listed).
  2. Claim list: columns as in ledger.py status plus attention. Quick filters: needs attention (none + stale), none, stale, hypotheses, Lean assumes, failed checks; text search over name and label; sort by any column and a "dependency order" sort (what a claim uses comes first). Checkbox per row, select all filtered, select all stale. A badge shows seen for claims marked seen (6).
  3. Detail: paper statement (KaTeX), Lean statement, back-translation (the leanreadings text), uses / used-by with status colours, attestation history, "why" (what makes it this status), checks, register, and the buttons Mark seen, Attest, Build review pack. For stale claims: what changed since the attestation (first version: the old and new bound hash and the list of changed inputs if ledger.py can name them; a text diff is a later ledger.py feature, see 11).
  4. Hypotheses tab: same list/detail for hypotheses, with the H1/H2 checklist and the cited source (link to downloaded_papers/ if the file exists, else DOI/arXiv from the citation).
  5. Attest dialog (single and batch, 6).
  6. Jobs panel: running and finished jobs with a live log.

docs.title: 6.1 Seen
docs.text: "Seen" is set only explicitly (button or key v) on the detail view of one claim. It is stored in the browser (localStorage) per claim and bound hash; a changed bound drops the marker. It is advice to the person, not a security boundary, and it is not written to the ledger.

docs.title: 6.2 Dialog
docs.text:
Fields: level (green/yellow/conjecture as ledger.py allows; yellow requires a reason), reason (multi-line; templates from signing.reasons, plus the last reasons used), checklist (checkboxes from [checklist.*] that apply to the targets), person and key (defaults from the config, key must be in keys.toml). Claims and hypotheses are not mixed in one batch (different checklists).

Preview table: claim, current attestation (level, date, current/STALE) -> new level, short bound, seen yes/no. Claims not marked seen are highlighted and listed in a warning. Confirming such a batch needs an extra step (type the number of unseen claims, or tick "I am attesting claims I have not marked as seen"). There is no block: the decision stays with the person. The reason text is shown above the table exactly as it will be signed.

docs.title: 6.3 Execution (server side)
docs.text: For each claim, in the order shown: 1. Re-read the ledger if any file changed; recompute bound from the current ledger, never take it from the browser. If the bound differs from the one the preview showed, skip that claim and report it. 2. Build the record as cmd_attest does (person, date = today, level, reason, checklist, bound); run L.checklist_problems. 3. Sign attestation_message(project, rec) with ssh-keygen -Y sign -n <namespace> -f <pubkey file>: the public key from keys.toml is written to a temp file, the private key stays in the agent. The tool never asks for a passphrase and never opens a private key file. Verify the signature with ssh_verify before writing. Agent not reachable or key not loaded: stop before the first claim with the exact ssh-add command to run. 4. Append to ledger/attestations.toml with toml_record, under a file lock, one claim at a time, so an interrupted batch leaves only whole records. A failure on one claim is reported and does not stop the others. Afterwards: reload, a result table (attested / skipped with reason / failed), and a one-line summary in the session log. Undo last batch removes the records this session appended while the file's tail is still exactly that text. Signatures are meant to be deliberate: one ssh-keygen -Y sign call per attestation, never a batched or cached signature. If the agent asks for confirmation per signature (ssh-add -c), that is intended; the dialog says up front how many confirmations to expect and the progress shows which claim is waiting.

docs.title: 7. Review packs
docs.text: Build review pack runs ledger.py [-P paper] review --for <selection or current claim> as a job (output directory from [review] out). On success the PDF opens in the embedded viewer (an <iframe> below the detail) or in the system viewer, per viewer.pdf. A pack records when it was built and from which bound hashes; the page shows "pack older than the statement" when a bound has changed since. Selecting claims and pressing the button builds one pack for exactly those claims, so the usual loop is: filter to stale, build the pack, read, mark seen, attest. Later: inline view of statement / back-translation / Lean text without LaTeX build (11).

docs.title: 8. Jobs
docs.text: status, lock, verify, check, extract, review run as subprocesses of ledger.py in the project root, one job at a time per kind, and only one Lean job at all (extract and anything that starts Docker Lean). extract is never started automatically and asks for confirmation (minutes of Docker). Output goes to a log streamed over Server-Sent Events; a job ends with status, duration and a reload of the view.

docs.title: 9. Formula rendering
docs.text: Statements, back-translations and Lean text are LaTeX fragments (Pandoc-style, \leandisplay{...}, \ensuremath{...}, \(..\), \[..\], environments). core/render.py: - collects \newcommand, \renewcommand, \DeclareMathOperator from the preamble of each paper's main file (balanced-brace parse; 32 macros in the current papers) and delivers them as KaTeX \defs (needed: \ket etc. clash with KaTeX built-ins); - adds the shim list: \mathds->\mathbb, \cite/\ref/\eqref placeholders, psmallmatrix, multline; - a fragment that fails to render is shown as source with a note and counted in the paper's counts, so a rendering gap is visible, not hidden. A script tools/render_check.py (the 9899-formula test, rewritten as a test) guards this.

docs.title: 10. Server API and security
docs.text:
Local only: bind 127.0.0.1; a random token per start in the URL fragment, sent as Authorization on every call; reject requests whose Host is not the bound address or whose Origin is present and different; no CORS headers; all JavaScript vendored (static/vendor/, with version and SHA-256 in VENDOR.md).

Method, path Writes Purpose GET /api/papers no papers with counts, titles, edition links GET /api/claims?paper= no claim view models GET /api/claims/{name} no detail incl. why, history, render macros GET /api/hypotheses?paper= no hypothesis view models GET /api/status no agent/key state, ledger warnings, changed-on-disk flag POST /api/attest/preview no validated preview table for a batch POST /api/attest yes execute a batch (6.3); needs token and a preview id POST /api/attest/undo yes undo the last batch of this session POST /api/jobs yes (runs commands) start a job from a fixed list, no free command strings GET /api/jobs/{id}/events no SSE log GET /api/packs/{id}.pdf no built review pack

Rules: no endpoint takes a path or command from the client; file names come from the ledger/config. The server logs every write to ledger-ui.log next to the config.

docs.title: 11. Changes to ledger.py (trust-ledger repo)
docs.text:
ledger.py may be changed for this tool; the changes are made in the trust-ledger repository (format version, tests and docs there) and then copied into ledger/vendor/ of a project as usual. Wanted, in order of need:

  1. Library API without sys.exit: sign_attestation, append_attestation (and ssh_sign) raise a LedgerError instead of exiting; cmd_attest becomes a thin wrapper. Needed by milestone 2.
  2. Structured status: status --json (claims, per tool states, attestation state with signature state, hypotheses, warnings), built from the same function as the text output. Then ledgerio.py calls this API instead of reading Ledger attributes; the version check stays.
  3. Stale diff: "what changed since the attestation of claim X": the inputs whose hash differs from the attested one and, for the statement, the old and new text. This needs the ledger to keep the attested inputs retrievable (an attestation only stores the bound hash today); the design of that (store the text in the attestation, or recover it from the previous lock file / a snapshot) is part of the task. Milestone 6.
  4. Batch attestation in the library (one reason, many claims, per-claim result) if it turns out cleaner there than in core/attest.py; the CLI could then offer it too.

Until a change exists, the UI uses the import-based fallback described in 2 and says what is missing.

docs.title: 12. Tests
docs.text: Pytest on the core with the examples/egg ledger of trust-ledger as a fixture (it ships keys and attestations; its private keys live in private/, so a test ssh-agent can sign for real). Cases: status view equals ledger.py status output; batch attestation writes records that verify accepts; a stale bound is skipped; an unloaded key stops the batch before the first claim; a half-written file never results. Server tests check token/Host/Origin handling. Rendering test as in 9. Browser behaviour is checked by hand for the first milestones.

docs.title: 13. Milestones
docs.text:
1. Done 2026-11-06: library API in trust-ledger (11.1, 11.2; and the agent-only signing fix, see below); Alpine and KaTeX vendored (static/VENDOR.md); config loader; core/ledgerio.py + ledger-ui --summary, tested against ledger.py status.
  2. Done 2026-11-06: server, token/Host/Origin/CSP, paper switcher + claim list + filters + sort + search, detail with KaTeX (statement, back-translation, Lean text, uses/used-by, attestation history, rests-on), changed-on-disk banner, deep links (?paper=&claim=). Not yet: checkboxes/selection (milestone 3), hypotheses tab (5), paper.toml titles/edition links (5).
  3. Done 2026-11-06: attesting through ssh-agent (core is already batch-capable: preview, signing job with per-claim progress, undo, session log ledger-ui.log); attest dialog for one claim, explicit "seen" marker (button / key v, kept in the browser per claim and bound hash), unseen warning with extra confirmation, key a opens the dialog. Hypotheses can be attested through the same API (UI in milestone 5).
  4. Done 2026-11-06: batch: checkboxes in the list, Select menu (all shown / stale / without attestation / shown-but-unseen / clear), "N selected, M seen", Next unseen (opens the next selected claim you have not marked), keys x select, j/k move, a attests the selection (or the current claim); one dialog for the whole selection; attested claims leave the selection afterwards.
  5. Done 2026-11-06: jobs (review, lock, verify, check, extract) with live log, cancel, one job per kind and one Lean job at a time; Review pack for the current claim or the selection (one paper at a time); embedded PDF viewer with a "statement changed since the pack was built" warning; Run… menu. Progress is polled (every 0.8 s), not streamed with Server-Sent Events: same effect, no long-lived connections.
  6. Done 2026-11-06: hypotheses tab (list with status, detail with the statement, cited sources as links, H-checklist, history, the claims proved given it; attest as a known theorem, same dialog, kind hypothesis; key t switches tabs); paper.toml metadata: title in the paper menu, links to the paper/reviewed/explained PDFs (only those that exist), warnings for a mismatching name/main. Phone layout (one column, fewer columns, no horizontal overflow) checked at 390 px.
  7. Done 2026-11-06: stale diff (see below); config bootstrap (ledger-ui --init path/to/ledger/ledger.toml writes ledger-ui.toml: finds a ledger.py, takes the first key of keys.toml; never overwrites). The "inline review view" is the detail page itself: statement, back-translation and Lean text are shown there without building a pack.

docs.title: 14. Notes from milestone 0
docs.text:
• ssh-keygen -Y sign -f KEY.pub falls back to the private key file next to the .pub when the agent lacks the key (and then asks for its passphrase on a terminal, which a server cannot answer). ledger.py ssh_sign therefore copies a .pub file into a scratch directory first; a key that is not in the agent is a LedgerError.

  • The vendored ledger/vendor/ledger.py of the paper project predates the API; until it is re-copied from trust-ledger, point [ledger] tool at the trust-ledger checkout.

  • Milestone 1: texlite.js renders every statement and back-translation of the nuclear, threshold and reach papers (136 texts, about 7000 formulas) with no failed formula and no unknown command. The ledger's statements are blocks [label] kind: [title] body; an equation/align block is the bare formula and is rendered as display math.

  • Alpine calls init() itself; do not also put x-init="init()" on the element (it ran twice and the second run lost the query string).

  • ledger.py got why_data / claim_detail (the detail view's data) in addition to status_data.

  • Milestone 2: the agent must hold the key before the batch starts (checked at preview and again at the start); the dialog shows the agent state and the ssh-add hint. Preview stores what will be signed on the server; POST /api/attest takes only the preview's id (single use, 20 minutes). An end-to-end browser test is tests/e2e/run_e2e.py (needs node, playwright-core and Google Chrome; not part of pytest).

  • A Unix socket path is limited to about 100 characters; test agents therefore live in short temporary paths.

  • Milestone 4: packs are built with --out <config dir>/.ledger-ui/packs/<job id>/, so the project's own review/ files are never overwritten; add .ledger-ui/ and ledger-ui.log to the project's ignore file. The PDF is fetched with the token and shown from a blob: URL (an iframe cannot send an Authorization header, and the token stays out of URLs). A pack for balanced in the nuclear paper takes about 10 s (the paper is built once, then the packet twice).

  • The stale warning compares the claims' statement hashes (bound) at build time with the current ones; it does not notice changes to the packet's other claims (what the targets rest on).

  • Milestone 5: a hypothesis whose statement is hand-written in a scope (text, because its paper is not part of that scope) has another bound than in the paper's own scope, so an attestation made there shows as stale in the other scopes (the nuclear paper's Banach lemma is current in -P nuclear, stale in -P reach). That is the ledger's rule, shown as it is.

  • Two section.detail elements exist now (claims, hypotheses): address them by id (#detail-claim, #detail-hyp).

  • Milestone 6, stale diff: no format change. ledger.py writes ledger/snapshots/<bound>.json whenever it attests (statement text, spec hashes and spec content of the evidence nodes and their declarations, statements of used claims); diff_since compares the latest attestation that has a snapshot with the current state: statement (word diff of the LaTeX source), claims it uses, and the changed evidence nodes field by field (Lean type, value). The page shows it for every claim or hypothesis that has a stale attestation, and offers "Record snapshots now" (ledger.py snapshot) for current attestations that have none. An attestation that is already stale and has no snapshot cannot be compared; the page says so.

  • The Egg end-to-end test found that POST endpoints which never read their body corrupted keep-alive connections (the next request was parsed as {}GET ...); the server now always consumes the body.

docs.text:
• \mathbb{1} for \mathds{1} looks different in KaTeX; check by eye at milestone 1.
  • Several projects in one config (list of [[ledger]]): the schema leaves room, not in the first version.

docs.title: Tests and screenshots
docs.text: The tool is developed against the trust-ledger repository, expected next to this one (or at $TRUST_LEDGER). Tests that need it use trust-ledger's public egg example on a scratch copy; nothing touches a real project.

docs.title: Unit and integration tests
docs.text:
uv sync
uv run pytest

They cover the configuration, access to ledger.py, rendering macros, signing with a real ssh-agent (a private agent is started per test), batches, undo, jobs, the HTTP server (token, Host and Origin checks, paths, keep-alive behaviour), and the two JavaScript modules under node (texlite.js, diff.js). Tests that need ssh-keygen, ssh-agent or node skip when they are missing.

docs.title: Browser test
docs.text:
tests/e2e/run_e2e.py drives the page in a real Chrome (attest, batch, hypothesis, jobs, snapshots, diff):

npm install playwright-core          # in any directory
uv run python tests/e2e/run_e2e.py --playwright DIR_WITH_node_modules --trust-ledger ../trust-ledger

docs.title: The screenshots of this manual
docs.text:
They are generated, not taken by hand, so they can be regenerated when the page changes:

uv run python tools/make_screenshots.py --trust-ledger ../trust-ledger --playwright DIR_WITH_node_modules

It builds a scratch project from the egg example (two invented people, one with a key loaded in a private agent), walks through the workflows and writes docs/images/*.png. Needs node with playwright-core, Google Chrome, and latexmk for the review pack picture.

docs.title: The manual
docs.text:
uv run mkdocs serve          # live preview at http://127.0.0.1:8000
uv run mkdocs build --strict
